job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Superintelligence Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Superintelligence Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Superintelligence Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COVERED AI SYSTEM.—The term "covered AI system" means—
  (A) an artificial intelligence model trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations in a single training run; or
  (B) any artificial intelligence system that the Secretary determines is capable of substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks.
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED FACILITY.—The term "covered facility" means a data center containing more than 50,000 advanced AI chips.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to train, develop, or deploy a covered AI system.
(b) EXISTING SYSTEMS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to a covered AI system whose training began before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) SAFETY EVALUATION.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered facility shall register the facility with the Department of Commerce.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the Department of Commerce a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the computing workloads run at the facility.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that covered AI systems can be developed safely.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**Drafting review: S. 2817, Superintelligence Prohibition Act (text as amended October 6, 2026)**

This review is based only on the text you pasted. I haven't checked it against the official amendment or the Congress.gov version, so verify section numbers and wording before publishing. The items are grouped by theme, and the first few are the most consequential.

**Internal conflicts and timing**

1. **Sec. 7(a) and 7(b):** Section 7(a) keeps the prohibition in force until Congress passes a joint resolution, but Section 7(b) ends the entire Act 10 years after enactment. The text doesn't say which controls, so the prohibition could lapse on a fixed date regardless of any congressional finding.

2. **Sec. 5(a) and Sec. 8:** The civil penalty covers violations "on or after the date of enactment," but Section 8 delays the Act's effect by 180 days. The penalty language should be aligned with the effective date.

3. **Sec. 3(b) and Sec. 8:** The grandfather clause protects systems whose training began before enactment, but the prohibition doesn't take effect until day 180. A training run started on day 1 is neither grandfathered nor yet prohibited, and the text doesn't say whether it must stop when Section 3 takes effect.

4. **Sec. 7(b) and Sec. 8:** Because the 10-year sunset runs from enactment rather than the effective date, the prohibition would operate for only about 9.5 years.

**Definitions and thresholds**

5. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** The 10^26 threshold has no measurement method. It doesn't say whether compute is actual or estimated, how precision is weighted, or how multi-stage or distributed training is totaled. Developers could split one effort into several "runs" to stay under the line.

6. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** The compute threshold is fixed in statute with no mechanism to amend it, and the Act gives no agency authority to update it. Algorithmic efficiency gains could let capable systems fall below the line over time.

7. **Sec. 2(1)(B):** "Secretary" is undefined. The Act doesn't say which Secretary makes capability determinations, and Section 6 separately refers to the Secretary of State.

8. **Sec. 2(1)(B):** "Substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks" has no benchmarks, determination procedure, notice requirement, or appeal path. This is a likely target for arbitrary-and-capricious or vagueness challenges.

9. **Sec. 2(1):** The definition mixes "AI model" (clause A) and "AI system" (clause B), but "system" is undefined. A sub-threshold model embedded in a larger system could be argued to fall either way.

10. **Sec. 2(2):** "U.S. person" covers citizens and state-law corporations only. It excludes LLCs, partnerships, and permanent residents abroad, and "State" is undefined, so it's unclear whether D.C. or territories count.

11. **Sec. 2 and throughout:** Several key terms are undefined, including "advanced AI chips" (Sec. 2(3)), "data center," "operator," "artificial intelligence," and "train, develop, or deploy." "Person" presumably takes the 1 U.S.C. § 1 Dictionary Act meaning, but the Act should say so.

**Scope of the prohibition**

12. **Sec. 3(a):** "Deploy" doesn't clearly reach API access, open-weight releases, hosting for third parties, providing compute, or possessing model weights. Each of these could be argued in or out.

13. **Sec. 3(a):** The compute test applies to "a single training run," so fine-tuning, distillation, or continued post-training of a sub-threshold model may fall outside the prohibition even if the result is comparable in capability.

14. **Sec. 3(a):** The "anywhere" reach over U.S. persons has no mechanism for enforcement abroad. Section 6's negotiation is the only stated route, and it doesn't create one.

15. **Sec. 3(c):** The safety-evaluation exemption depends on "the purpose of" the activity, which is undefined and hard to prove or disprove. It has no requirement for registration, qualified evaluators, scale limits, output controls, or time limits. It also doesn't say whether it covers training itself or only testing, making it the most significant gap for developers seeking to continue large training runs.

16. **Sec. 3(b):** "Training began" is undefined. It could mean first compute reservation, data preparation, or the first gradient step.

17. **Sec. 3(b):** Because the exemption is drafted as a carve-out from subsection (a), it appears to cover development and deployment of the grandfathered system, not just the continuation of training. It also doesn't limit retraining or require documentation.

**Registry (Sec. 4)**

18. **Sec. 4 and Sec. 5:** The Act creates no penalty for failing to register or report. Section 5 penalizes only violations of Section 3, so the registry is effectively unenforceable as written.

19. **Sec. 4(b):** "Computing workloads" is undefined. Reports aren't required to identify which models were trained or their compute, so the registry can't verify compliance with Section 3.

20. **Sec. 4(b):** The quarterly certification has no false-statement penalty beyond general federal law, and no mechanism for Commerce to audit or verify submissions.

21. **Sec. 2(3) and Sec. 4:** The 50,000-chip threshold applies per "data center," with no aggregation rule for affiliates, adjacent sites, or leased capacity. An operator could structure facilities to fall under the threshold.

22. **Sec. 4:** The section sets no initial registration deadline, no procedure for Commerce to act on reports, and no confidentiality protections for reported information.

**Penalties and enforcement (Sec. 5)**

23. **Sec. 5(a):** The Act doesn't name an enforcing agency or a cause of action. It's unclear whether DOJ, Commerce, or a private party enforces the civil penalty.

24. **Sec. 5(a):** The Act gives no injunctive authority, investigative power, or subpoena power, so there's no clear way to stop an ongoing violation or obtain evidence.

25. **Sec. 5(a):** "Each day" is undefined for continuing violations, and the $1 million per-day amount isn't tied to revenue or compute. The Act also doesn't state a limitations period, so the general default would apply.

26. **Sec. 5(b):** "Willfully" is undefined, and the Act says nothing about corporate criminal liability or responsible-officer liability. It also doesn't address what knowledge the defendant must have about whether a system crosses the compute threshold.

27. **General:** The Act has no severability or savings clause. Courts generally presume severability, but if Section 2(1)(B) or Section 3(c) is struck for vagueness, the absence of a clause leaves more room for dispute over what survives.

**Duration and international provisions**

28. **Sec. 7(a):** The NASEM report has no deadline and no required content, and "developed safely" is undefined. It's also unclear whether the joint resolution must go to the President under Article I, Section 7, which should be stated if intended. The Act doesn't say what happens if NASEM never reports.

29. **Sec. 7(a):** "Covered AI systems" in the joint resolution could mean the whole class or specific systems, and the text doesn't say which.

30. **Sec. 6:** "Shall seek to negotiate" imposes no obligation beyond trying. It has no reporting requirement, no consequence for failure, and no definition of "equivalent." The 18-month window also ends after the Section 3 effective date.

**Implementation and judicial review**

31. **General:** The Act gives Commerce measurement, registration, and reporting duties but no rulemaking authority and no appropriation. Staff should check whether funding appears in a separate bill.

32. **General:** The Act has no judicial review provision, so challenges to capability determinations or registry actions would rely on default Administrative Procedure Act standards.

33. **General (constitutional flag):** Restrictions on deployment and possibly on releasing model weights may raise First Amendment questions, and the criminal provisions may face due process vagueness challenges. These are issues for legal review, not conclusions I can draw from the text.

**Before publishing**

- Confirm the section citations and wording against the official amendment.
- Consider sending items 1–4, 15, and 28 to a congressional counsel or CRS analyst before the markup, since they bear most directly on whether the bill operates as written.
- Note that these are drafting observations. Some gaps would help developers, while others would make enforcement or defense harder for any party, so the piece should describe them neutrally.
